title: Jeremiah 44:1–14
context: The LORD speaks through Jeremiah to the Judeans living in Egypt, at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and Pathros. He reminds them that Judah fell because of incense offered to other gods despite the prophets’ repeated warnings, and asks why they repeat the same sins in Egypt. Judgment will reach them there as it reached Jerusalem, and only a few will escape to return. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about the persistence of idolatry and God’s patient warnings.

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews who lived in the land of Egypt, who lived at Migdol, and at Tahpanhes, and at Memphis, and in the country of Pathros, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans living in Egypt, at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and in the land of Pathros. The community has spread.

Arminian readers see God addressing his scattered people wherever they are.
verses.reformedNotes:
Migdol and Tahpanhes are usually placed in the north, Memphis farther south, and Pathros in Upper Egypt, though exact locations are debated.

Reformed readers see God’s word reaching the diaspora. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘You have seen all the evil that I have brought on Jerusalem, and on all the cities of Judah. Behold, today they are a desolation, and no man dwells in them,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD of Armies reminds them that they have seen the evil brought on Jerusalem and Judah’s cities, now desolate and empty. History is evidence.

Arminian readers see the people invited to learn from recent events.
verses.reformedNotes:
The appeal to what they have seen grounds the oracle in shared experience.

Reformed readers see God interpreting history through his word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about learning from the judgments God has already brought, so that they need not be repeated.

verses.text: because of their wickedness which they have committed to provoke me to anger, in that they went to burn incense, to serve other gods that they didn’t know, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.
verses.arminianNotes:
The disaster came because of the wickedness of burning incense and serving gods they had not known. The cause is named.

Arminian readers see judgment linked to the people’s chosen idolatry, carried on across generations.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘that they didn’t know’ emphasizes that these gods had no history of saving them.

Reformed readers see idolatry as the root of Judah’s fall. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of turning from the LORD to other gods.

verses.text: However I sent to you all my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them, saying, “Oh, don’t do this abominable thing that I hate.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD sent his servants the prophets repeatedly, pleading, “Oh, don’t do this abominable thing that I hate.” God warned earnestly.

Arminian readers see God’s persistent appeals as sincere invitations to turn.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘rising up early’ pictures God’s urgent, repeated sending of prophets.

Reformed readers see God’s long patience displayed through the prophets. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s earnest warnings before judgment.

verses.text: But they didn’t listen and didn’t incline their ear. They didn’t turn from their wickedness, to stop burning incense to other gods.
verses.arminianNotes:
They did not listen or turn from their wickedness or stop burning incense to other gods. The warnings were ignored.

Arminian readers see a deliberate, repeated refusal of God’s appeals, which the people were responsible for.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse summarizes the response to generations of prophetic preaching.

Reformed readers see the hardness of the human heart. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the consequences of persistent refusal to listen to God’s messengers.

verses.text: Therefore my wrath and my anger was poured out, and was kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem; and they are wasted and desolate, as it is today.’
verses.arminianNotes:
So the LORD’s wrath was poured out on Judah and Jerusalem, leaving them desolate as they are today. Judgment followed refusal.

Arminian readers see judgment as the consequence of the people’s refusal to heed repeated warnings.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘as it is today’ ties the oracle to the visible ruin of the land.

Reformed readers see God’s justice displayed in history. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the reality of judgment after long patience.

verses.text: “Therefore now the LORD, the God of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Why do you commit great evil against your own souls, to cut off from yourselves man and woman, infant and nursing child out of the middle of Judah, to leave yourselves no one remaining,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks why they commit great evil against themselves, cutting off man and woman, infant and nursing child, leaving no remnant. Their actions harm them.

Arminian readers see God pleading with them to consider their own good.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question shows that sin harms the sinner and the community.

Reformed readers see God’s concern even in rebuke. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the self-destructive nature of idolatry and God’s appeal for the people to consider where their path leads.

verses.text: in that you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, burning incense to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have gone to live, that you may be cut off, and that you may be a curse and a reproach among all the nations of the earth?
verses.arminianNotes:
They provoke God with incense to other gods in Egypt, so that they will be cut off and become a curse among the nations. The pattern continues abroad.

Arminian readers see the people repeating in Egypt the sins that ruined Judah.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse links the community’s present worship with its likely future.

Reformed readers see sin following the people wherever they go. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the persistence of idolatry and its consequences.

verses.text: Have you forgotten the wickedness of your fathers, the wickedness of the kings of Judah, the wickedness of their wives, your own wickedness, and the wickedness of your wives which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks whether they have forgotten the wickedness of their fathers, the kings of Judah and their wives, and their own and their wives’ wickedness. Memory is called on.

Arminian readers see a call to remember and learn.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse names the whole community, including the royal household and the women, preparing for the exchange in 44:15–19.

Reformed readers see shared guilt across generations. Both traditions read this as shared ground about remembering past sin.

verses.text: They are not humbled even to this day, neither have they feared, nor walked in my law, nor in my statutes, that I set before you and before your fathers.’
verses.arminianNotes:
They have not been humbled, feared, or walked in God’s law and statutes, even to this day. The heart is unchanged.

Arminian readers see the absence of repentance after judgment, despite every opportunity to turn.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse describes a failure to respond to judgment with humility.

Reformed readers see the hardness that judgment alone does not cure. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the need for humble repentance and obedience to God’s law.

verses.text: “Therefore the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I will set my face against you for evil, even to cut off all Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says he will set his face against them for evil, to cut off all Judah. The judgment is announced.

Arminian readers see God’s settled response to persistent rebellion among those in Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes:
‘All Judah’ here refers to the community in Egypt, as the following verses show; verse 14 allows for a few who escape.

Reformed readers see God’s justice against unrepentant sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground and read the verse together with verse 14.

verses.text: I will take the remnant of Judah that have set their faces to go into the land of Egypt to live there, and they will all be consumed. They will fall in the land of Egypt. They will be consumed by the sword and by the famine. They will die, from the least even to the greatest, by the sword and by the famine. They will be an object of horror, an astonishment, a curse, and a reproach.
verses.arminianNotes:
The remnant who set their faces toward Egypt will be consumed by sword and famine, from least to greatest, becoming a horror and a curse. The warning of chapter 42 is repeated.

Arminian readers see consequences matching their choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The language closely echoes 42:17–18.

Reformed readers see God’s word fulfilled as spoken. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the consistency between God’s warning and its fulfillment, and they hear the verse soberly.

verses.text: For I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will punish those in Egypt as he punished Jerusalem, by sword, famine, and pestilence. The comparison is direct.

Arminian readers see that leaving the land did not escape the consequences the people feared.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse parallels Jerusalem’s fall with the coming judgment in Egypt.

Reformed readers see the consistency of God’s justice. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the futility of fleeing God’s word and the seriousness of continuing in the sins that brought Jerusalem’s fall.

verses.text: so that none of the remnant of Judah, who have gone into the land of Egypt to live there, will escape or be left to return into the land of Judah, to which they have a desire to return to dwell there; for no one will return except those who will escape.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
None of the remnant in Egypt will escape to return to Judah, as they long to, except a few who escape. A small exception remains.

Arminian readers see a thread of mercy in the mention of survivors.
verses.reformedNotes:
The final clause qualifies the sweeping language; 44:28 also speaks of a few who return.

Reformed readers see God preserving a remnant even in judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground about judgment with a narrow hope.
